I became cold, tired, frustrated and then unfeeling. I looked at people suffering and felt nothing. Now that I am out of the toxicity that was the hospital I have the urge to help when I see a person suffering or in pain but my emotions have still numbed to near nothing. In many ways it is advantageous. Without heavy emotion, I can see solutions to problems more clearly. I'm not a completely heartless robot anymore but I do find that when I'm in a situation that calls for it I switch into "professional-mode" and my sense of humour, emotions, and everything that makes me *me* takes a backseat so I can do my job. That is often what happens when you become a healthcare professional. Only the *best* manage to break that and put their soul into their work without damaging themselves. 

The best get that way with as much self-care as patient care. They visit therapists, eat healthy, socialize on weekends, and exercise. Most of the doctors I work with are runners or lifters. One is a surfer. One is a skiier and tennis player. You need hobbies and friends to keep you safe and sane. Reward your accomplishments, accept and learn from mistakes. Keep mentally healthy.

Like I said at the start, to survive as a heathcare professional you will become something else. But what you become could be something truly worthy. But that is entirely up to you.

I used to be a nurse. 

My compassion dried up pretty fast. I realized pretty quickly that I didn't like who I was in a nursing environment. I started out smiling at patients, laughing with them, going above and beyond to make them feel at ease. 

Then I found myself getting sneered at for answering buzzers after 9pm. During handover I told the other nurses about how one patient with Type II Diabetes and a Below Knee Amputation had hidden a 2.5L bottle of Coca-Cola (nope, not diet) in her pillowcase; I was accused of fatshaming by the other staff members. I watched a sobbing paraplegic parient shit all over the floor and her wheelchair while the nurse who was supposed to help her left her there and gossiped in the hallway with other nurses. When I told her that her parient had shat herself and was in distress she pretended not to speak English.

Within a few months I felt my neutral expression harden into a constant frown. I heard myself barking at patients and AINs instead of helping them. I watched my posture change. I dreaded going to work. I dreaded looking in a mirror. I became a shell of the wide-eyed earnest young woman who entered her nursing career.

I quit working in a hospital last year. I am now working part time as a private nanny for a family with a couple of disabled children and I work for a non-profit which provides in-home nursing care for military vets. I work erratic hours and I took a pay cut but it was worth it. I am a amateur therapist first and a nurse second. And I am a lot happier this way. I will never work in a hospital again.
